baer-heitev/1:א: (א) Shehecheyanu. And if he did not say it on day one, he blesses on day two or on one of the other days when he remembers; and if he has no cup of wine at the time of Kiddush he blesses shehecheyanu without a cup, and it appears to me that even if he blessed initially and did not bless on the second day of Yom Tov of the diaspora he blesses all seven — Magen Avraham. And Kaf HaChayyim wrote it appears the same applies to Shavuot, even though it is only two days, nevertheless it has make-up all seven. And further it appears to me that if he forgot to say shehecheyanu on the first night and on the second night said shehecheyanu, he need not say shehecheyanu again based on the first night to complete it — for if the first day is holy, then he completed shehecheyanu on the second day, and if the second day is holy, behold he said shehecheyanu — Kaf HaChayyim, see there. And if he forgot to say Kiddush at night, his law is as above siman 471 seif 8, and so too Eliyah Rabbah seif 485. And if he forgot to say the Haggadah he has no make-up at all, as it is written "because of this" at the hour when matzah and maror are placed before you, and so too Magen Avraham below siman 485 see there. And they do not say "who performed miracles for us" because he is destined to say it in the Haggadah — Tur and Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/1:ב: (ב) On Shabbat. It is permitted to say the Haggadah from a book even though he is alone, and we are not concerned that perhaps he will lean, as written siman (479) [475] seif 9. Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/1:ג: (ג) He makes havdalah. And if he remembered in the middle of the meal that he did not make havdalah, he makes havdalah in the middle of his meal over the cup; and if his intention was to drink wine during the meal he does not bless borei peri hagafen, and if it was not his intention he must bless, and he should not wait to make havdalah until after the meal, for then it would be like adding to the cups; and it is better that he say havdalah and Hallel on one cup, for one cannot have two sanctifications on one cup — only Kiddush and havdalah are permitted, for both are one matter; and if he forgot to make havdalah until after birkat hamazon he says Hallel and havdalah on one cup, for one cannot [do so] on another matter. Magen Avraham, and see above siman 296:
baer-heitev/1:ד: (ד) Kiddush. See Acharonim on this. And the essence is as Rama ruled, so agreed Taz, that one who sees him washing hands thinks he will also bless al netilat yadayim as during the rest of the year; but in truth it is forbidden to bless, since this washing is not for eating matzah, for it is a great interruption, and so is custom:
baer-heitev/4:א: (א) Afterward. It is good to have live and cooked [vegetables] over which one blesses borei peri ha'adamah, as written siman 203; and custom is to take what they call parsley. And it is good to take karpas, which is a notarikon: 60 (sixty) ten thousands worked hard labor, and they call it in foreign tongue epich; and so Acharonim, and see Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/4:ב: (ב) Salt water. And if [Pesach] falls on Shabbat he should make the salt water from erev Shabbat; and if he did not make it from erev Shabbat and has no vinegar he should make a little salt water, as written siman 321, Taz. And Magen Avraham wrote, and it appears to me that after he ate the vegetable it is permitted to remove the vegetable and salt water from the bowl:
baer-heitev/4:ג: (ג) For the chagigah. Even if it falls on erev Pesach on Shabbat. And see in Rosh what he wrote in the name of Mahari of Orleans and Mahari of Corbeil that their words are the opposite of the Gemara, and see Yad Efraim on this:
baer-heitev/4:ד: (ד) And he arranges. The order of the bowl of the Ari is copied from Etz Chayim, and thus: the order of the guarded [matzot] shall be in this order — one takes three guarded matzot and places Kohen on top, then Levi, and below him Yisrael, corresponding to the three mochin of Abba Ilaa; afterward one takes maror, karpas, charoset, and two kinds of cooked dish — a roasted lamb shank and a boiled egg — and places these five things above the three matzot: namely the shank, which was kindness at your right, and the egg, which is gevurah at your left; maror, which alludes to tiferet, in the middle between the shank and the egg, for tiferet mediates between kindness and gevurah; afterward charoset on the right line under the shank because it alluded to netzach; afterward karpas, which alludes to hod, place under the egg on your left line; afterward take chazeret and place below the maror on the middle line corresponding to yesod, in order to make afterward a korech with chazeret. And the bowl itself that includes them all is malchut — behold the ten sefirot of chochmah; and one should not change this order, and fortunate is one who intends for the above — end quote:
baer-heitev/4:ה: (ה) Shank. And there should be a little meat on it. Darkei Moshe:
baer-heitev/4:ו: (ו) Roasted. They eat it because it was a remembrance of mourning, but roasted meat they do not eat, and such is custom; and see Taz. And if he forgot to roast the meat or the egg on erev Yom Tov he should not roast at night unless his intention is to eat that night and day. Maharil and see Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/5:א: (א) Chazeret. It is lettuce; olshin is coriander; tamcha is horseradish. Custom spread to take horseradish for maror and bless on the leaves; and the stalk one takes for korech. In responsa Chacham Tzvi siman 119 he wrote: the chazeret mentioned in our Mishnah is the vegetable called in foreign tongue salad and in Spanish salad, and it has the signs mentioned in the Gemara; and because in Ashkenaz lands it is not found at Pesach time they did not become accustomed to take it for maror and take horseradish, which is tamcha, and one fulfills with it — though they cannot eat even half a kezayit because of its sharpness — and they nullify the mitzvah of maror — end quote, see there. And I also heard from one foreigner that in a hot country lettuce is found in Nissan days and is double and thick like what we call in these lands head lettuce, and they eat that species for maror; and see Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/5:ב: (ב) In the root. Meaning small roots that split here and there, but the large root on which the vegetable stands is included in the stalk. Maharil, and see Taz:
baer-heitev/5:ג: (ג) For a kezayit. For it is like half a chicken egg, and this measure is required in full apart from the space between the leaves, as written siman 486; and one should be careful about this, for otherwise it is a berachah lebatalah, since he blesses on eating it and eating implies a kezayit. One who is ill or fastidious may take for himself whichever kind of maror is most palatable to him; and if it is impossible for him altogether, in any case he should eat a little or chew in his mouth for remembrance of bitterness of taste without a berachah, and it is fit to push himself with all his ability even if it pains him to fulfill a mitzvah of the Sages, as written above siman 474 seif 10:
baer-heitev/5:ד: (ד) Bitter vegetable. Even though one cannot [bless] on another matter, in any case one should bless only on these species enumerated in the Mishnah, and so agreed Shach and Magen Avraham. Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/5:ה: (ה) Vinegar. And Pesach that falls on Shabbat — one must put the liquid in it from erev Shabbat; and if he forgot, one may do so through shinui, namely that he put the liquid first in the vessel and afterward put charoset in it, as written siman 321 seif 16, and so Magen Avraham; and see there in Taz sk 10 that he forbids putting ground baked matzah to mix with wine or honey water on Shabbat even through shinui, and his words are not compelling; also the world is not careful about this. Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/5:ו: (ו) For straw. And one should not grind it well so that [the pieces] be long. Beit Yosef:
baer-heitev/6:א: (א) He washes. For anything whose dipping is in liquid requires washing; and Taz wrote: from here is clear proof against those who are not careful all year to wash hands for things dipped in liquid — how is this night different from all nights of the year? And if he comes to purify himself more on this night, at least he should be careful also on days of repentance; but here there is only lack of care and they do not scrutinize to equalize their measures — end quote. And Eliyah Rabbah in siman 85 wrote the world is accustomed not to wash and they have on what to rely, that Tosafot hold so, and so Magen Avraham siman 158 see there; and that they wash on this night is like one of the other changes made this night so that they will ask. Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/6:ב: (ב) Less. For if he eats a kezayit there will be doubt whether he blesses birkat hamazon — Tur; therefore if it happened that he ate a kezayit he should not bless birkat hamazon. Taz and Magen Avraham, Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/6:ג: (ג) For afikoman. And the larger portion he hides. Acharonim. Also it is fit to wrap in a cloth and place between the pillow and mattress, and when he wishes to eat he takes it out as it was in the napkin and drapes it behind him and walks about four amot and says: thus were our ancestors going with their leftovers tied in their garments — Rashal. And see Kaf HaChayyim siman 474 sk 2 — reason for custom that children take the afikoman:
baer-heitev/6:ד: (ד) The bowl. With everything on it, and one need not remove the cooked dishes. Tur:
baer-heitev/6:ה: (ה) Ha lachma. Some say ha kolachma — see Magen Avraham. And Maharshal wrote siman 88 to say it in a loud voice:
baer-heitev/6:ו: (ו) To remove them. And now they are not accustomed to remove them because children have no recognition in this that they know these things were not placed on the table for the purpose of eating. Magen Avraham:
baer-heitev/6:ז: (ז) And they will ask. And he tells them they are not permitted to eat until they tell of the Exodus from Egypt; therefore one should not place any matzah on the table until after the seder. Maharil:
baer-heitev/7:א: (א) Why is this night different. One should not say "we are obligated to dip," etc., but rather "we dip," for it is not an obligation but only for recognition — Tur. When he says "and it is this that stood for our fathers," etc., until "the Holy One, blessed be He, saves us from them," he should hold the cup in his hand. And when he says "and we will say before Him song," it must be v'ne'emar with segol vowels (under the alef), which is past tense, referring to the redemption from Egypt that has passed. Bach, Rashal, Shelah:
baer-heitev/7:ב: (ב) For maror. But when he reaches "the Pesach that our fathers," etc., he should not hold it in his hand, for it is like raising consecrated things outside [the Temple], but nevertheless he should look at it. Maharil siman 193:
baer-heitev/7:ג: (ג) With his finger. Written in Hagahot Minhagim that one should sprinkle with the small finger, namely the pinky; and Magen Avraham wrote one should sprinkle with the ring finger, which is next to the small, for with the ring finger the Holy One, blessed be He, struck Egypt. And in Darkei Moshe he wrote one should take specifically with the index finger in remembrance of what is said "it is the finger of the Almighty," and such is the essence. Kaf HaChayyim:
baer-heitev/7:ד: (ד) In his hand. In the text of the berachah "who redeemed us" Maharil wrote: when Pesach falls on Shabbat one should reverse and say first "from the Pesachim" and afterward "from the sacrifices," for the chagigah does not override Shabbat, and on the second night the opposite — see there. And in Pesach Me'ubin siman 268 he wrote one should say everything in one text "from the sacrifices and from the Pesachim," and Acharonim agreed, such as Maharil, and so Bach. In saying Hallel one should not sit reclining but with awe and fear — Shelah. Levush wrote they are not accustomed to bless on Hallel since they divide half before the meal and half after. A blind person is obligated in reading the Haggadah, and when he reaches "this matzah" and "this maror" he does not say "this" but says "the matzah we eat," etc. — Kaf HaChayyim sk 39:
beer-hagolah/1:ב: (ב) So it implies daf 103 regarding washing hands
beer-hagolah/1:ג: (ג) Sefer Abudraham in the name of his teacher
beer-hagolah/2:ב: (ב) Tur in siman 474 in the name of Rav Sherira, Rav Hai, Rosh, and R. Yitzchak
beer-hagolah/3:ב: (ב) Kol Bo in the name of R. Yehonatan
beer-hagolah/4:א: (א) Tur in siman 479 in the name of Tosafot and Rosh
beer-hagolah/4:ג: (ג) Tur, there, in the laws of Pesach.
beer-hagolah/5:ב: (ב) Hagahot Maimoni in the name of Rabbenu Tam and Semag
beer-hagolah/6:ג: (ג) Rosh there, R. Yitzchak, and Shulchan Pesach, and responsum of Maharil — in order to remove himself from the dispute of poskim on birkat hamazon
beer-hagolah/6:ד: (ד) Rosh and Mordechai and Shulchan Pesach
beer-hagolah/6:ו: (ו) Rosh in responsum and Shulchan Pesach
beer-hagolah/6:ז: (ז) There in chapter 115, and so Tosafot and Rashbam there
beer-hagolah/7:ב: (ב) Tur from that which "bread of affliction," etc., 115
beer-hagolah/7:ד: (ד) Tur in the name of custom of Ashkenaz and Shulchan Pesach
machatzit-hashekel/1:_: (s"k 1) Sheheheyanu, etc. It should read: even if he blessed, etc., and did not bless on the second Yom Tov, etc.; Kaf HaChayim wrote: but he did not bless on the first Yom Tov night and blessed on the second night — he fulfills necessarily: if the first Yom Tov was weekday he certainly need not bless sheheheyanu except the second night; and if the first was Yom Tov, he completed with what he blessed on the second night — since the first was Yom Tov, the second weekday, he need not bless sheheheyanu on the second night for the second night; and the berakha he blessed on the second night ascends to complete the first day.
machatzit-hashekel/2:א: (א) (s"k 2) And afterward, etc. Since there is a dispute in siman 499 whether one who makes havdalah during the meal must recite borei peri hagafen on the havdalah cup.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ב: (ב) And if he did not have in mind to drink wine during the meal — in such a case all agree he must recite on every wine he drinks during the meal, all the more so the havdalah cup.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ג: (ג) And one should not say havdalah and Hallel on one cup. To say Birkat HaMazon and havdalah on one cup is explicit in the Gemara daf 102 — forbidden because two sanctifications on one cup appear as if the mitzvot are burdens on it; Magen Avraham added the same for Hallel and Hagadah — why on one cup?
machatzit-hashekel/2:ד: (ד) And if he forgot, etc. he says Hallel and havdalah on one cup; and likewise if he remembered during Birkat HaMazon that he did not make havdalah, he recites Birkat HaMazon and havdalah on one — what is the difference? Rather since Magen Avraham deals with whether to say Hallel and havdalah on one cup, he also cites here Hallel and havdalah.
machatzit-hashekel/3:א: (א) (s"k 3) And one should not, etc. It implies he holds it forbidden, etc.; since he wrote "but all year it appears," etc., he had to give a reason if one washes before kiddush — it implies preferable if one washes after kiddush; in siman 471 there is dispute among poskim on this.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ב: (ב) And the reason the Gemara explains, etc. He abbreviated greatly the reason of Beit Shammai, who hold it forbidden to use a vessel whose back is impure though its inside is pure, for the reason explained there; therefore Beit Shammai hold one must wash before pouring — if he pours first, perhaps sparks at pouring will fall on the back of the cup and receive impurity from hands that are impure before washing — they are second [degree], and the liquids become first [degree] and then defile the back of the vessel; though a vessel does not receive impurity except from a father of impurity, nevertheless rabbinically a vessel receives impurity from impure liquids even if the liquids are only first — therefore he washes hands first so they be pure. Beit Hillel hold it is permitted to use a vessel whose back is impure; therefore one must pour first — if he washes first, perhaps at pouring his hands are not dry and water is "touching in order to touch"; perhaps the vessel's back is impure and liquids on his hands receive impurity from the back and return to defile the hands. And further, even for Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel hold even if forbidden to use a vessel whose back is impure, preferable to pour first so pouring not be an interruption between washing and ha-motzi — thus far the Gemara.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ג: (ג) Therefore it appears to me, etc. Meaning: Maharil's intent is not as Darchei Moshe understood — Maharil brought in Sefer Avraham Rokeach: if one washes before kiddush it appears the law is like Beit Shammai who washes and then sanctifies — end of his words. If so, Maharil does not mean Beit Shammai require washing before kiddush; rather Beit Shammai must hold one need not be concerned for interruption between washing and ha-motzi — otherwise he would agree with Beit Hillel to pour first, for Beit Shammai's concern of back-impurity is only a slight concern and interruption is certain; or Beit Shammai hold even if interrupting between washing and ha-motzi it does not matter; but we hold like Beit Hillel that interruption is forbidden — nevertheless all year one who washes before kiddush has no interruption concern, for kiddush is not an interruption — only pouring is interruption, as Tosafot brought Magen Avraham in siman 166 that they poured in hot water; care needed not to omit or add water — see there; but on Pesach there is great interruption between washing and ha-motzi in Hagadah — certainly an interruption like pouring; and although immediately after kiddush he needs washing for dipping, and washing before kiddush could rise for dipping — nevertheless people will not understand he washes for dipping, since all year they do not wash for things dipped in liquid; they will err that he washes for ha-motzi and this is interruption like pouring; they will think the law is like Beit Shammai who are not concerned for interruption — such is Maharil's intent per Magen Avraham; and what Magen Avraham concluded "and all agree on this" — even Beit Shammai who hold pouring is not interruption nevertheless agree Hagadah and Hallel are interruption; and what Maharil wrote "then it appears like Beit Shammai" — even if for Beit Shammai it is interruption, one may say people will err that Hagadah interruption is only like pouring interruption, and as pouring is not interruption for Beit Shammai, so Hagadah.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ד: (ד) And Maharshal, etc. before kiddush so as not to change from all year.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ה: (ה) Bach wrote: nevertheless wash again for dipping, for he holds kiddush is an interruption in the complete sense between washing and ha-motzi — not that kiddush is interruption, since kiddush requires a meal — there is no kiddush except where there is a meal — they are considered one; unlike dipping, which has no need for kiddush — kiddush is the interruption.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ו: (ו) If so it appears contradictory; therefore if he washes before kiddush it is not evident he washes for dipping, only as all year when one washes before kiddush even though afterward he washes again for ha-motzi — nevertheless it is not so evident; see Taz s"k 6 and Kaf HaChayim.
machatzit-hashekel/4:א: (א) (s"k 4) And karpas, etc. arduous labor; I heard from a great man who knew through investigation in medical books that karpas is what we call celery — through meat they improve; but if cooked alone without meat it would change for the worse; at least they would not improve — nevertheless one recites on it raw borei peri ha-adamah, as siman 200.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ב: (ב) I would say, meaning: even if surprising that even without meat they improve through cooking, nevertheless since in any case it is also eaten raw, one recites when raw borei peri ha-adamah.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ג: (ג) There is dispute — Tur and those who disagree; also one authority is unclear to me in Magen Avraham — apparently Maharil's father holds and doubts whether cooked is preferable even cooked without meat; for on maror too one recites borei peri ha-adamah — from the law in siman 475 seif 2: if he lacks vegetables for first dipping he takes maror and recites borei peri ha-adamah — see there.
machatzit-hashekel/5:_: (s"k 5) Salt water, etc. for that meal it is permitted; nevertheless forbidden to put two-thirds salt and one-third water — see there.
magen-avraham/1:א: (א) Sheheheyanu. And if he did not bless on the first night he blesses all seven; and the same for every Yom Tov (Eruvin daf 40); and it appears to me that even if he blessed on the first and did not bless on the second day of Yom Tov of the diaspora, he blesses all seven.
magen-avraham/1:ב: (ב) And afterward he makes havdalah. If he remembered in the middle of his meal that he had not made havdalah, he makes havdalah in the middle of his meal on the cup; and if he had in mind to drink wine during the meal he does not recite borei peri hagafen, since there is a dispute — doubtful berakhot to be lenient — see siman 499 s"k 3; if he did not have in mind he must bless and should not wait until after the meal, for then it is like adding to the cups; and one should not say havdalah and Hallel on one cup, for two sanctifications on one cup are impossible — only kiddush and havdalah are permitted, since both are one matter, as Pesachim says: also in havdalah we say "who distinguishes between holy and holy"; if he forgot havdalah until after Birkat HaMazon he says Hallel and havdalah on one cup, for it is impossible otherwise, as siman 494 s"k 3.
magen-avraham/1:ג: (ג) And one should not wash the hands, etc. For if they wash before kiddush it implies they act like Beit Shammai, who hold kiddush requires washing; but all year it appears he washes for the meal, and although here too dipping after kiddush requires washing, nevertheless it should not enter people's minds that he washes for dipping and they think he washes for kiddush — end of Darchei Moshe in Maharil's name, who implies it is forbidden to wash oneself before kiddush (and see Orach Chayim 12); nevertheless I do not know where we find Beit Shammai hold kiddush requires washing — only in Berakhot chapter 8 they dispute: Beit Shammai: wash hands then pour the cup; Beit Hillel: pour then wash; the Gemara explains because of impurity and purity for Beit Hillel, because of interruption between washing and ha-motzi — therefore it appears we hold like Beit Hillel, and only pouring is interruption as Tosafot Arvei Pesachim, but kiddush is not interruption; on Pesach, where there is great interruption, they wash close to the meal — and all agree on this; Maharshal: take water before kiddush and wash hands, and not wash again for dipping; Bach: nevertheless wash again for dipping; I am not persuaded — as Maharshal, for all year we do not wash for dipping, so it appears contradictory — Abudraham siman 188.
magen-avraham/4:א: (א) And karpas. Maharil wrote: custom to take karpas, notarikon: sixty ten thousands did arduous labor; his father was unsure whether permitted to take parsley because it is better cooked than raw — then no borei peri ha-adamah, as siman 200 — end; I wonder why our countries are accustomed to take parsley; perhaps they hold through meat they improve, as written; and per what is written in the name of Tur — only when not eaten at all raw does one recite she-hakol; but when eaten raw, even if better cooked, nevertheless one recites when raw borei peri ha-adamah — if so, no difficulty; still my view wavers why they chose something disputed — he should take another vegetable; perhaps other vegetables are not so available on Pesach, or because in the Gemara vegetables are mentioned and other things are called lefet, and our vegetable is not eaten raw unless pickled, unavailable on Pesach; Tur and Gemara say one also recites on maror borei peri ha-adamah — maror there must have been fit to eat raw like latukh — see there.
magen-avraham/4:ב: (ב) Salt water. Hagahot Maimoniot: if Pesach is Shabbat make salt water on erev Shabbat; but siman 321 s"k 2: whatever is needed for that meal may be done on Shabbat; it appears after eating the vegetable it is permitted to remove vegetable and salt water from the plate.
magen-avraham/4:ג: (ג) Above everything. Meaning: close to it.
magen-avraham/4:ד: (ד) Forearm (zeroa). Ran wrote: bone without meat is not called a cooked dish; therefore a little meat should be attached (Darchei Moshe).
magen-avraham/4:ה: (ה) On the coals. For the Pesach was roasted only on a pomegranate skewer and trouble to return to it (Beit Yosef, Hagahot Maimoniot); forbidden to eat, for one does not eat roasted on Pesach nights; therefore forbidden to roast it on Yom Tov, for Yom Tov does not prepare for another day; it appears if he forgot to roast until night he roasts at night and eats it morning of the first Yom Tov; Maharshal wrote to cook a piece of meat and divide among those reclining; so Bach and Shlah; if he does not wish to eat the egg until the second night, likewise forbidden to roast it the first night (Darchei Moshe, Mahari"v) — see 503.
magen-avraham/5:א: (א) Chazeret. Latukh; Levush wrote it is called in Polish zarzich.
magen-avraham/5:ב: (ב) Endives (olashin). Korvil; krishfla in Arabic; andibi in Spanish (Hagahot Maimoniot).
magen-avraham/5:ג: (ג) Tamcha. Krien; in foreign tongue maertikh; Maharil was unsure whether korvil is maror; in foreign tongue marubya; charchevina: palm shoots.
magen-avraham/5:ד: (ד) Not from the root. Mahari"v: if taking maertikh, take what is above ground, leaves and adjacent parts, not below ground, which is root — end; so Mishna Berurah and Shlah; but earlier Mahari"v wrote in first chapter of Sukkah: they said hyssop three stalks with three pods — Rashi: stalks are roots; from this it appears what Rabbenu Tam wrote "not roots" means small roots branching, but the large root the vegetable stands in is included in stalk — end; Hagahot Maimoniot: I heard stalk is called until below its tail and small spikes emerge — end; and so is essential: the world recites on leaves and for korekh takes the stalk; it appears the reason: since it says one fulfills with its stalk, leaves are preferable — therefore leaves for berakha; nevertheless need a kezayit, siman 486; because leaves are not so plentiful, take stalk for korekh; but if he wishes leaves for korekh, permission is his.
magen-avraham/5:ה: (ה) Whether moist. It implies one does not fulfill with wilted; so Tur and Rambam — see Gemara.
magen-avraham/5:ו: (ו) Not pickled. Rashi: in vinegar; it appears he follows his view as Beit Yosef Yoreh De'ah 105; but we hold something in water from the eve is pickled like cooked — if maror soaked from the eve one does not fulfill, bitterness nullified; see Beit Yosef siman 527 — Mahari"v: Maharar"a was unsure — since maror is compared to matzah and stolen is invalid, perhaps a Jew should not uproot maror from the ground, siman 649; it appears not comparable — there lettuce is sustained in earth therefore like earth — end; it appears since maror is not sustained in earth it is like movable property, gentile acquisition through despair and change of domain, change of domain in Israel's hand; still difficult, for we hold whatever is attached to ground is like ground, siman 637 s"k 3, especially rooted in ground Yoreh De'ah 6:2 and Choshen Mishpat 95 and 193; perhaps when maror was already fully cooked and stands to be uprooted, he holds whatever stands to be uprooted is considered uprooted.
magen-avraham/5:ז: (ז) Or another bitter vegetable. Shibolei HaLeket: Gemara proves one fulfills only with those enumerated; what Agur wrote to take wormwood — he explains maror is wormwood; if so, other bitter vegetables he eats without berakha — the Mechaber's words require study — end; it appears the truth is Agur's intent, for Agur wrote so in Maharil's name: one without latugi — some say the earlier in the mishnah is earlier for the mitzvah; there the four species are mentioned in foreign tongue (as above); Tashbetz: take vermet in foreign tongue, maror of the mishnah; reason: some reverse the order — therefore if no chazeret, for all maror is preferable; Agudah: take maertikh, tamcha; perhaps because olashin/korvil was not clarified — siddurim say korvil for first dipping, implying not maror — thus Maharil and Agudah; also maror is vermet; known wormwood is vermet in Ashkenaz; in Minhagei Maharik where no latugi they take wormwood called verimda or other bitter thing — Tashbetz — end; if so, maror of the mishnah includes all bitter vegetables; so Rashi in Chumash: any bitter herb is maror; but Gemara does not imply so; also Sukkah 13: even field bitterness one does not fulfill because it has a qualifying name — must be called maror without qualifier; also Rashi's intent seems all are called maror, nevertheless one fulfills only those called maror at matan Torah; therefore no berakha on other vegetables.
magen-avraham/5:ח: (ח) A little vinegar. If Shabbat, put liquid from erev Shabbat (Agudah) — see 321:16: through change permitted to put liquid on Shabbat — put liquid first then charoset.
magen-avraham/5:ט: (ט) Similar to straw. Not ground well and they are long (Beit Yosef, Rokeach); Maharil: do not grind them — they should be long.
magen-avraham/6:א: (א) Less than a kezayit. For if he eats a kezayit there is doubt whether he recites a concluding berakha (Tur); therefore if he happened to eat a kezayit he does not recite a concluding berakha.
magen-avraham/6:ב: (ב) And he recites borei peri ha-adamah. Before dipping so it precede the act; the same for maror (Maharil); difficulty — the berakha refers only to eating, borei peri ha-adamah, and so for maror — requires study.
magen-avraham/6:ג: (ג) And he breaks it in two. For it requires lechem oni — a poor person's way is with a piece.
magen-avraham/6:ד: (ד) And he gives half. Meaning: the larger half (Maharil, Bach).
magen-avraham/6:ה: (ה) Under the cloth. Some place it on their shoulders in remembrance of the Exodus.
magen-avraham/6:ו: (ו) And he lifts the plate. And need not remove the cooked dishes (Tur).
magen-avraham/6:ז: (ז) Ha Lachma Anya. Biblical language, as written "so they will see the bread that I fed them," etc.; do not corrupt the formula to k'Ha Lachma or Ha Kolachma (Mahariv, Darchei Moshe, Mateh Moshe) — some do not want Ha Lachma because it is not the very bread Israel ate; proof from scripture "the bread that I fed" — yet that bread they already ate, only a sample of bread; here we bake new matzot — not fit to say Ha Lachma; therefore one who says Ha Kolachma or k'Ha Lachma did not lose.
magen-avraham/6:ח: (ח) And he commands to remove them. Now they are not accustomed, for children lack recognition — they know these were not placed to eat; in Gemara times they were accustomed to clear the table.
magen-avraham/6:ט: (ט) And they will ask. Tell them they may not eat until the Exodus is told; therefore no matzah on the table until after the seder (Maharil).
magen-avraham/7:א: (1) Mozgin, etc. He will not say, "We must baptize, etc., we shall be baptized, but we shall know before the babies, only he shall say, We are baptized (Tur), when it is said, "She who stood for our fathers," etc., he shall hold the cup in his hand and cover the brim until he saves us from their hands (Shal. Rashel of 2015):
magen-avraham/7:ב: (2) with his finger It is customary to throw with one's finger because the finger of the Omnipresent is a dalah kamash in the Hagman to throw with a small zerat akal dm. And Bilkot P. Vara cites chapters of RA that with the ring finger the Holy One, blessed be He, is the Egyptians and in this verse it is said that the finger of the Omnipresent is and therefore one must throw with the ring finger:
magen-avraham/7:ג: (ג) Sixteen times. Corresponding to the sword of the Holy One, blessed be He, called yud-heh-vav-heh (Darchei Moshe).
magen-avraham/7:ד: (ד) He covers the bread. Lest he see his nakedness, as siman 471:9; when Pesach is first day of Yom Tov say from the Pesach offerings and from the sacrifices — they did not offer the festival offering, for festival offering does not override Shabbat (Bach, Mahari"v) — see Tur.
mechaber/1:main: Laws of the first cup and the Pesach seder until the second cup. Containing 7 seifim:(1) They pour for him the first cup (1) and make kiddush on it (1) and recite (2)(1)(2)(1) sheheheyanu (3) and if it falls on (2)(2) Shabbat he says Vaykhulu, and if on Motza'ei Shabbat (4)(3) he says yaknehaz (3) and if he forgot havdalah and did not remember until he began the Hagadah (5)(4) he completes the Hagadah until Ga'al Yisrael (2)(6)(5) and afterward (3) makes havdalah: {Rama: (1)(7)(6)(7)(8) And one should not wash the hands at all before (4) kiddush (Rabbi Yerucham and the Rash in responsum and Mordekhai chapter Arvei Pesachim) and if his hands are not clean (7) he washes a little (8) but does not recite on the washing; and the master of the house (8) should not pour for himself (9} — only another pours for him in the manner of freedom (Mahariv)}
mechaber/2:main: (4)(9)(10) He drinks reclining (5)(2)(11) and does not recite a berakha after it.
mechaber/3:main: (6)(12) If he wishes to drink several cups (10)(13) permission is in his hand (7)(14) nevertheless (15) it is fit to be careful (16) not to drink between the first and second unless for great need (11)(17) so he not become intoxicated and be prevented from performing the seder and reading the Hagadah.
mechaber/4:main: (8)(18) They bring before the master of the house a plate (19) containing three matzot and maror (20) and charoset (4)(12) and karpas (21) or another vegetable (5) (and vinegar (3)(13)(22) or (5)(6) salt water) (9)(1) and two cooked dishes, one in remembrance of the Pesach offering and one in remembrance of the festival offering; custom: meat and egg: {Rama: (23) And he arranges the plate before him so he need not pass over the matzot — karpas on top of all, vinegar closer than matzah, matzot before maror and charoset, and they closer than meat and egg (Maharil); custom: meat is the forearm (zeroa}; meat roasted on coals, egg cooked (and likewise roasted — so in our city)}
mechaber/5:main: These are the vegetables with which one fulfills his obligation:(11)(2)(33) chazeret (10) endives (11) tamcha charchevina (34)(meaning species of bitter herbs) (35) maror — one fulfills with their leaves and with their stalks (12)(5)(36) but not with the root (13) only that with leaves one does not fulfill (19)(37) unless they are moist, and with stalks one fulfills (13) whether moist or dry (14)(20)(38) but (14) not pickled (39) nor scalded nor cooked (40) and all (21) combine (13)(41) to a kezayit, which is their measure (15)(22)(42) and the essential mitzvah (43) is with chazeret; if he lacks chazeret (16)(44) he returns after first to first per the order they are listed: {Rama: (45) if he lacks (46) one of these vegetables (47) he takes (23) wormwood (15)(24)(48) or another bitter (14) vegetable (Agur) (25) and charoset (49) he makes thick in remembrance of clay and afterward they put in it (16)(26)(50) a little (15) vinegar or red wine in remembrance of blood (Tur) and they make charoset from fruits with which Israel were compared (Tosafot chapter Arvei Pesachim) (51) such as apples, figs, nuts, pomegranates, almonds, and they put on it spices such as cinnamon and ginger (17)(27)(52) similar (16} to straw with which they kneaded the clay (Tur)}
mechaber/6:main: (18)(41)(7)(42)(8)(43) He washes hands for first dipping (44)(18)(45) and does not recite on washing (46)(9)(47)(18)(48) and takes from karpas (19)(8)(18)(49) less than a kezayit (50) and dips in vinegar (19)(51) and recites borei peri ha-adamah and eats (29)(52) and does not recite after it; takes the middle matzah (20)(53)(20)(30)(54) and breaks it in two (21)(55) and gives half to one of those reclining to guard for afikoman (19)(56) and they place it under the cloth (22)(57) and the other half between the two whole ones (21)(23)(31)(58) and lifts the plate (22)(59) with the matzot and says (32)(24)(60) Ha Lachma Anya until Mah Nishtanah: {Rama: (62)(63) say in a language (2)(64} women and children understand, or explain; R' Yitzchak of London did entire Hagadah in vernacular (Kol Bo and Mahariv)} (23)(25)(33) then commands (26) to remove them from the table (65) and place at the end as if already eaten so children see (26)(66) and ask:
mechaber/7:main: (24)(27)(67)(34) Immediately pour the second cup (68)(69) so children ask why a second cup before the meal; if the son lacks wisdom the father teaches; if no son, his wife asks; if not, he asks himself; even scholars ask one another (9)(24)(35) Mah Nishtanah, etc. (70)(when son or wife asks, need not say Mah Nishtanah but begin Avadim) (Maharil) (25)(71) when beginning Avadim, i.e., to Pharaoh, return the plate with matzot and read all Hagadah (26)(72) when reaching "this matzah" raise to show (small: raised broken matzah, lechem oni) (Mahari"v) (36)(73) likewise "this maror" (27)(74) when reaching Lefichak each raises his cup until concluding Ga'al Yisrael: {Rama: custom to sprinkle a little from the cup (28)(37)(26)(75) with his finger (opinion) at blood, fire, smoke; likewise plagues dtzach adash b'achav (28)(76) sixteen times (Maharil) (77) bread uncovered (38)(39) while saying Hagadah until Lefichak (40)(27)(78) when holding cup (79) then cover bread (30}(Agur and Beit Yosef)}
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (א) And he makes kiddush on it — before kiddush intend to fulfill kiddush and four cups, kiddush cup being one of four; some say "I am ready to sanctify and fulfill four cups" — careful not to say this after kiddush since he already blessed borei peri hagafen on the cup, only before kiddush; before Hagadah intend or say to fulfill telling the Exodus [Chayei Adam]. Sheheheyanu — before drinking; if not before drinking, bless whenever he remembers day one, even in the market, time is rolling; if remembered on second night after sanctifying the day, exempt with sheheheyanu on the cup after kiddush; if forgot sheheheyanu on second night's kiddush, even if already blessed first night, obligated whenever remembers through the festival until end of last diaspora Yom Tov; likewise other Yom Tov until festival end.
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (ב) On Shabbat — permitted to say Hagadah from a book even alone; we are not concerned he may tilt, as explained above siman 475:9 — see there.
mishnah-berurah/1:ג: (ג) He says yaknehaz — meaning: first wine berakha and kiddush and ner, i.e., borei me'orei ha-esh and havdalah and sheheheyanu; do not bless on spices every Motza'ei Shabbat to Yom Tov; say havdalah seated like kiddush.
mishnah-berurah/1:ד: (ד) He completes, etc. — to make havdalah immediately when remembered he cannot, for havdalah requires a cup and the one who blesses must taste; during Hagadah forbidden to interrupt with drinking; from the Mechaber's wording "until he began Hagadah" implies if remembered before Hagadah he need not wait but immediately pours a cup and says havdalah berakha and drinks — however this is only per the Mechaber who does not bless on each cup; per Rama 474 gloss and our custom to bless each cup, he must bless borei peri hagafen — then it appears like adding cups, forbidden, as siman 472:7; therefore possibly even if remembered before Hagadah there is no remedy until completing Hagadah, unless at time of first cup blessing he will drink between cups as siman 472:7 — see Bi'ur Halakha. If forgot Hagadah at night — no compensation, for "because of this" when matzah and maror before you; if forgot kiddush at night — law as siman 471:8.
mishnah-berurah/1:ה: (ה) And afterward makes havdalah — bless borei peri hagafen on second cup and also ner and Yom Tov havdalah and drink; if remembered mid-meal he did not make havdalah, must interrupt immediately and make havdalah, not borei peri hagafen, for second cup drunk before eating exempts unless he then had no intent to drink during eating — then also borei peri hagafen; if remembered during Birkat HaMazon — Birkat HaMazon and havdalah on one cup; if not until after cup of Birkat HaMazon — wait until after Hallel and Hagadah, then havdalah on fourth cup; if not until after fourth — havdalah on fifth cup and must bless borei peri hagafen since he already removed his mind from drinking [later authorities].
mishnah-berurah/1:ו: (ו) And one should not wash, etc. — meaning: even those who all year wash before kiddush for the meal — for them kiddush is not interruption between washing and meal as explained siman 471 — nevertheless on Pesach night, where they interrupt much after kiddush in Hagadah and lose attention to guarding hands, all agree not to do so; even to wash so as not to need wash again after kiddush for karpas is also not proper per later authorities.
mishnah-berurah/1:ז: (ז) He washes a little — wrote "a little" to heed the reason Darchei Moshe brought: do not wash before kiddush lest it appear kiddush requires washing — therefore not a full washing.
mishnah-berurah/1:ח: (ח) But do not bless, etc. — even if full washing, careful not to bless al netilat yadayim, for this washing does not count for eating — berakha in vain.
mishnah-berurah/1:ט: (ט) Only another pours for him — if possible.
mishnah-berurah/2:א: (א) He drinks reclining — if forgot and did not recline, see siman 472:7 and Mishna Berurah s"k 21.
mishnah-berurah/2:ב: (ב) And does not bless after it — on the vine, etc., even if drank a revi'it — relies on Birkat HaMazon at end; also will recite concluding berakha after four cups — explained well siman 474.
mishnah-berurah/3:א: (א) Several cups — whether between first and second or after second cup, even during eating; but between third and fourth forbidden, as below siman 479.
mishnah-berurah/3:ב: (ב) Permission is in his hand — per Mechaber below 474 gloss: our custom first berakha on each cup — permitted to drink between cups only if at berakha time he intended to exempt all he would later drink [or wine was before him, automatically exempt if he did not explicitly decide not to drink]; if no intent to drink between cups and later decided to drink — must bless; forbidden, appears like adding cups since he blessed this cup like the four — as written siman 472 s"k 21 in Mishna Berurah.
mishnah-berurah/3:ג: (ג) It is fitting to be careful — and such is our custom [Darkei Moshe]:
mishnah-berurah/3:ד: (ד) Not to drink between the first and second [cup] — to be concerned for the opinion of someone who says (and it is brought in Beit Yosef) that what we permit to drink between the cups is only between cup 2 and cup 3, which is close to the meal or during the meal, for then one does not become intoxicated; but not between the first and second, so that one should not become intoxicated, and as it is forbidden between the 3rd and 4th:
mishnah-berurah/3:ה: (ה) So that one should not become intoxicated — it implies specifically wine or other beverages of this kind that intoxicate; but a beverage that does not intoxicate, it is permitted to drink between the cups:
mishnah-berurah/4:א: (א) They bring before the master of the house — but before the other members of his household they need not arrange in this order; rather all take from the master of the house's [portion]. This applies even in places where there is a small table before each one, and all the more so in our place where all sit on one table:
mishnah-berurah/4:ב: (ב) That it has three matzos — two for lechem mishneh as on other Yom Tov, and one in order to break it into two: half of it to fulfill therewith the mitzvah of eating matzah, for the Merciful One calls it "bread of affliction," and the way of a poor person is in a piece and a half; the second for afikoman, as explained below in seif 6:
mishnah-berurah/4:ג: (ג) And charoset — in order to dip the maror therein, as below in siman 475. And karpas is a type of vegetable called karpas, and they chose l'chatchila this species because it is a notarikon: sixty [times ten thousand], meaning six hundred thousand performed hard labor:
mishnah-berurah/4:ד: (ד) Or another vegetable — of any species; but l'chatchila it is good to take from that species over which one recites that berachah that one recites over maror, so that he should exempt through this the maror that he eats during the meal; but he should not take for this one of the five species of maror, for after he has filled his belly with maror how can he afterward bless on eating maror — and see below in siman 475 seif 2:
mishnah-berurah/4:ה: (ה) Or salt water — to dip therein the karpas and the vegetable. If it falls on Shabbat he should make the salt water before Shabbat and not make it on Shabbat, as written in siman 321 seif 1; and if he did not make it before Shabbat and he has no vinegar to dip therein, salt water should be made in small quantity, as written there. And behold, the matter of dipping the vegetable in liquid is a rabbinic enactment, in order to astonish the children so they see a change — that they eat vegetables by dipping, which is not their manner to eat them before the meal throughout all the days of the year — and they will ask about this change, for the obligation of reciting the Haggadah is to say it as an answer to questions that were asked him, as it is said: "when your son asks you," etc., "and you shall say to your son: we were slaves," etc.:
mishnah-berurah/4:ו: (ו) A remembrance of the festival offering — and if [the first day of Pesach] falls on Shabbat, some say one need take only one cooked dish corresponding to the Pesach, for the festival offering does not come then since it does not override Shabbat; and some say that nevertheless one must make two cooked dishes as in other years, and the Sages did not distinguish in this, since it is only a mere remembrance — and such is the custom:
mishnah-berurah/4:ז: (ז) And they are accustomed with meat and egg — and all the more so if he wishes to make two types of meat, one roasted and one cooked, as a remembrance of the Pesach and the festival offering, for that is fine; rather that he also fulfills through the egg. And some wrote that what they chose an egg — meaning, the Merciful One seeks to redeem us. And some wrote because we make a remembrance of the mourning for the Temple, for we are unable to offer the Pesach sacrifice:
mishnah-berurah/4:ח: (ח) In a manner that he does not need, etc. — meaning that he should not need to skip them:
mishnah-berurah/4:ט: (ט) Above, etc. — meaning next to it:
mishnah-berurah/4:י: (י) And they should be closer, etc. — and some wrote that one need not be strict about the meat and egg if he will need to skip them, since they are not a mitzvah but a mere remembrance; and also regarding maror and charoset it is possible that "one does not pass over" does not apply — and see in the Acharonim the order of the seder plate of the Ari z"l:
mishnah-berurah/4:כ: (20) Arm - because of the bent arm that the Omnipresent showed in Egypt. And the one who does not have an arm will take the rest of the meat even without the bone [Peri Megadim] The judges wrote in their opinion that there should be a little meat on the arm which is reminiscent of the meat of the Passover sacrifice:
mishnah-berurah/4:ל: (ל) It should be roasted — and not cooked, as a remembrance of the Pesach sacrifice:
mishnah-berurah/4:מ: (מ) On the coals — and even though the Pesach was ideally roasted on a spit, nevertheless since it was only roasted on a pomegranate-wood spit, which requires trouble to turn it around, therefore it suffices for us with roasting on coals, which fulfills from the essence of the law also for the Pesach sacrifice [Magen Avraham]:
mishnah-berurah/4:נ: (נ) And the egg should be, etc. — since it is a remembrance of the festival offering, which does not require roasting:
mishnah-berurah/4:ס: (ס) And the same applies if roasted — for the festival offering comes whether roasted or cooked:
mishnah-berurah/4:ע: (ע) And thus is our custom in our city — to roast the egg. And it is forbidden to eat the [meat of the] foreleg at night, for one does not eat roasted [meat] at night; but the egg, even though it is roasted, is permitted, for there is no prohibition of roasted [meat] on an egg; and therefore it is forbidden to roast the foreleg at night except m'b'eod yom (before nightfall), unless his intention is to eat it tomorrow on that day; and therefore if he forgot and roasted it at night, he should be careful to eat it tomorrow morning — so wrote Magen Avraham and other Acharonim; and if his intention is not to eat the egg until the second night, the egg too is forbidden to roast at night except m'b'eod yom. Chayei Adam wrote: evil is this practice that they throw away the foreleg, and it is disgrace to a mitzvah. And it is a mitzvah to leave [it] on the second Yom Tov morning into the roast that they roast for Yom Tov, and they eat it:
mishnah-berurah/5:א: (א) For his obligation — meaning for the obligation of the mitzvah of maror, to fulfill what is written: "upon matzos and bitter herbs shall they eat it"; and now that we have no Pesach, matzah and maror are only d'rabbanan. Just as one does not fulfill with stolen matzah, as above in siman 454, so one does not fulfill with stolen maror; and therefore one should be careful that a Jew should not uproot the maror himself from a gentile's land, even if he gives him permission, for generally gentiles are land-thieves; and abandonment does not apply to land, as below in siman 649 seif 1 in the Hagah — rather the gentile should uproot it himself, and then abandonment applies there, and afterward the Jew acquires it from him, for there is through this abandonment and change of ownership:
mishnah-berurah/5:ב: (ב) Meaning: types of bitter herbs — all of them are referred to; and because we do not know clearly which they are in our language, therefore he wrote in general "all of them," that they are bitter species; and the Acharonim wrote that tamcha is chrain in our language, and on chazeret wrote Chayei Adam, and likewise Chafetz Chaim which is what we call salatin:
mishnah-berurah/5:ג: (ג) Maror — it is also a species of bitter vegetable known to them by the name maror, on account of that it is very bitter:
mishnah-berurah/5:ד: (ד) But not in the root — meaning: small roots that branch to here and to there at its base or at its sides; but the large root in which the vegetable stands is the stalk. And behold, in our countries the other species are not found, and therefore the maror customary in our country to eat is tamcha (and it is chrain); and one should be careful not to eat it when it is whole, for it is nearly a danger and there is no mitzvah in it, for because of its sharpness it is greatly harmful; therefore one must grate it on a grater and leave it thus exposed, and then it mitigates its sharpness. And the Gra instituted not to grate it before his coming from the synagogue, so that he should not mitigate the taste, for then one does not fulfill with it; rather he should grate it after his arrival and cover it until the beginning of the seder [and when Pesach falls on Shabbat he should grate it m'b'eod yom and place it in a vessel and cover it until the beginning of the seder] and then he should scatter it on the plate and thereby mitigate its sharpness; and then he should crush it and estimate that there should be a k'zayit, and he can eat it properly:
mishnah-berurah/5:ה: (ה) Unless they are moist — dried ones have no taste of maror and behold they are as mere dust; not so in the stalk, for since it is thick, even if it is dry it does not lose its taste. And wilted leaves — some say one fulfills with them, and some are strict even with wilted ones:
mishnah-berurah/5:ו: (ו) But not pickled — that is, if he soaked them in water from the outset; and some say specifically if he pickled them in vinegar; and therefore l'chatchila one should be careful not to soak the chrain in water from the outset, and b'dieved one may rely to be lenient when he has no others, because in chrain we see that there is still in it taste of maror. And it appears to me that with leaves one should not be lenient, for possibly through pickling from the outset in water the taste of maror emerges in them. And know that one fulfills with leaves even l'chatchila. And behold, I have seen many weak people who press themselves to fulfill the mitzvah of maror with stalks, and I do not know why they do not take the leaves for the mitzvah — perhaps because dry and wilted ones are commonly found in them. However, if they are moist, one should not be strict in this at all:
mishnah-berurah/5:ז: (ז) And not boiled/softened — greatly boiled and boiled in the manner of cooking — all because they have no taste of maror through this:
mishnah-berurah/5:ח: (ח) And all of them, etc. — meaning all five species mentioned; and we do not say that since every vegetable certainly has a bitter taste by itself they do not combine, for the taste of one is nullified in its fellow — it teaches us that since in any case all of them have a taste of bitterness, they combine [Ran]:
mishnah-berurah/5:ט: (ט) To a k'zayit — it is the measure of half an egg (and see below siman 486); and if he fulfills the mitzvah with leaves, he should see to press them together, for the space between the leaves does not combine to a k'zayit; and one should be careful in this, for otherwise it is a berachah in vain, since he blesses on eating and eating implies a k'zayit; and also he does not fulfill therewith the mitzvah of maror:
mishnah-berurah/5:י: (10) (MB) in hazrat - which is a reminder of the slavery of Egypt which had a soft beginning and at the end was hard, and yes, he created a horseradish that started sweet and ended bitter, and his last writings are even more precious than the rest of the bitter ones. (Shakorin Kharayan) even though it is third per the order that they are different because the Omnipresent forbid it fails because of the existence of a Durbanan, and in particular it is possible to have both of them by Timka:
mishnah-berurah/5:כ: (כ) He should seek first first — and one who is ill or delicate is permitted to take whichever species is more pleasant to him; and he may also eat the k'zayit little by little within the measure of k'vei'achalat peras, for per the essence of the law one fulfills thus, as below siman 475 seif 6; and if even so it is impossible for him because of his health, at minimum he should eat a little or chew in his mouth to remember the taste of bitterness, but he should not bless on this:
mishnah-berurah/5:ל: (ל) One of these vegetables — meaning the five mentioned:
mishnah-berurah/5:מ: (מ) He should take wormwood — see in Biur Halachah:
mishnah-berurah/5:נ: (נ) Or other bitter vegetable — those that have the signs mentioned in the Gemara regarding maror, that it should be fit for eating, and that it has sap (meaning: when they cut it, at the place of the cut white sap comes out like milk), and its leaves are pale (meaning its leaf is not very green like the leaves of onions and other vegetables, but leans somewhat to whiteness); nevertheless regarding berachah one should not bless on them, because we are not so expert in these signs:
mishnah-berurah/5:ס: (ס) He should make it thick — and make it m'eve Yom Tov; and if he forgot, it is permitted to make it on Yom Tov:
mishnah-berurah/5:ע: (ע) A little vinegar — of wine or red wine, in order to soften it and it shall be a remembrance of blood. If it falls on Shabbat he should put the liquid in it from erev Shabbat; and if he forgot, see above in siman 321 seif 16 and in Mishna Berurah there seif kaf 68:
mishnah-berurah/5:פ: (80) (Matt) such as apples - according to what is written under the apple, you have been awakened, as well as the rest of the fruits, all of which are written in the Song of Songs and almonds in the name that the Almighty the Omnipresent chose to make:
mishnah-berurah/5:צ: (צ) Resembling straw — that they are not ground well and they are long:
mishnah-berurah/6:א: (א) For the need of the first dipping — as he explains and continues. And the reason is that everything whose dipping is in liquid requires netilah, as above in siman 158:
mishnah-berurah/6:ב: (ב) And he should not bless, etc. — as the Mechaber ruled above in siman 158 seif 1; and see there in Mishna Berurah the opinion of the Gra on this matter:
mishnah-berurah/6:ג: (ג) Less than a k'zayit — because with a k'zayit there is doubt in the blessing acharonah whether he should bless it or not; therefore it is better that he eat less than a k'zayit so there should be no obligation at all according to all:
mishnah-berurah/6:ד: (ד) In vinegar — or in wine or in salt water, and this comes only to exclude that he should not dip in charoset, for charoset is only for the second dipping when one dips the maror in charoset [Beit Yosef]:
mishnah-berurah/6:ה: (ה) And he blesses Borei peri ha'adamah — and he should intend to exempt through this berachah also the maror that he will eat afterward [Acharonim]:
mishnah-berurah/6:ו: (ו) And he does not bless after it — even if he ate a k'zayit, because the first berachah stands also for the maror, as above; and therefore the Grace after Meals that exempts the maror that he eats during the meal stands also for the karpas that he ate earlier — and see in Biur Halachah what he wrote in the name of the Gra on this:
mishnah-berurah/6:ז: (ז) The middle one and he breaks it into two — in order to fulfill what the verse called "bread of affliction," and the way of a poor person is in a piece; and he said "the middle one" because the berachah of eating matzah primarily applies to it, and the berachah of HaMotzi that he blesses at the beginning applies to the upper one placed before him:
mishnah-berurah/6:ח: (ח) And he gives half, etc. — so that the two eatings that he eats for the sake of matzah should be in a piece; and it is good that that portion should be larger [Acharonim]:
mishnah-berurah/6:ט: (ט) Under the cloth — a remembrance of what is said "their leftovers tied in their garments"; and some place it on their shoulders as a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt. And they should be careful to wrap the afikoman in a cloth that was not laundered with k'rachma'al, for cloths are generally laundered with k'rachma'al [Chayei Adam]:
mishnah-berurah/6:י: (י) And he raises the plate — with everything that is on it, and he need not remove the cooked dishes:
mishnah-berurah/6:כ: (כ) Ha lachma anya — and some say k'ha lachma anya. And he must say it in a loud voice:
mishnah-berurah/6:ל: (ל) And he says in the language, etc. — meaning from Ha lachma anya onward, which is the beginning of the Haggadah:
mishnah-berurah/6:מ: (מ) In a language that they understand, etc. — and he fulfills therewith what the verse said "and you shall tell your son," etc.:
mishnah-berurah/6:נ: (50) (Sed) So that the women understand - after all, women are also obligated to recite the night mitzvah and to recite the Haggadah, etc., in the sign of Ta'ab Sidd, and therefore the obligation is also on the maid to sit at the table and listen to the entire Haggadah, and if they have to go outside to cook, she is obligated to hear the Kiddush, and when he comes to the rabbi, he says whatever he did not say, etc. Ten plagues that the Omnipresent brought upon Egypt to tell them how many miracles the Omnipresent had done for Israel [8]:
mishnah-berurah/6:ס: (ס) And to place them at the end of the table — and if the table is small, remove them entirely from the table, for otherwise there is no change for the child [Eliyah Rabbah]:
mishnah-berurah/6:ע: (ע) And they will ask — the matzos prepared for eating: why do we remove them? And he says to them that they are not permitted to eat until he tells of the Exodus from Egypt. Maharil wrote that one should not place any matzah on the table until the time of the meal:
mishnah-berurah/7:א: (א) Immediately — meaning that he should not wait in mixing the cup until he reaches "therefore," for then he needs to hold the cup in his hand; rather immediately when he removes the plate from the table he mixes:
mishnah-berurah/7:ב: (ב) Second cup — and he need not rinse and wash, for they already rinsed for Kiddush:
mishnah-berurah/7:ג: (ג) So that they will ask, etc. — meaning and thereby he will be aroused to ask further questions and wonders that he sees on that night:
mishnah-berurah/7:ד: (ד) And when the son or the woman asks — and the same applies if one Torah scholar asks his fellow; the one asked need not say "why is this night different":
mishnah-berurah/7:ה: (ה) And he reads the entire Haggadah — and one should not say it reclining, only in awe and fear [Shelah]. When he says "and we shall say before Him song," it must be "v'ne'emar" with segol vowels under the alef, and "ne'emar" is past tense, for it refers to the redemption from Egypt [Acharonim]:
mishnah-berurah/7:ו: (ו) And likewise when he reaches "this maror" — but when he reaches "the Pesach that our forefathers," etc., he should not hold in his hand the meat that is a remembrance of the Pesach, for it is as raising consecrated [meat] outside [the Temple precincts], for it appears from this that he consecrated it for the Pesach. Mordechai wrote that one must say "and we shall eat there of the sacrifices and of the Pesach offerings," for they eat first of the festival offering, which is the sacrifice; but the Pesach is eaten on the full [stomach]:
mishnah-berurah/7:ז: (7) (Ag) And when he comes to the conclusion of Magbia, etc. - and in the Omnipresent's time he wrote a model when the Piscah is said and she is the one who stood for our ancestors and for us until the Almighty saves us from them, he will hold the cup in his hand and then the mouth will be covered when he holds the cup in his hand:
mishnah-berurah/7:ח: (8) (at) with his finger - it is customary to throw with the finger because the finger of the Omnipresent is weak as a reference to the custom of throwing a small finger:
mishnah-berurah/7:ט: (9) (Eh) 16 times - against the 16th letters of the name of the Omnipresent who struck Pharaoh:
mishnah-berurah/7:י: (י) And the bread should be uncovered, etc. — for therefore matzah is called "bread of affliction," that one answers upon it matters:
mishnah-berurah/7:כ: (כ) That he holds the cup in his hand — in order to say song over the wine:
mishnah-berurah/7:ל: (ל) And then he covers the bread — so that his nakedness should not be seen, as is written siman 471 seif 9:
turei-zahav/1:_: One should not wash hands before Kiddush. Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Mordechai: it is permitted to wash hands before Kiddush, for it is not diversion of attention; but on Pesach, where there is a great interruption in between, Beit Yosef should not wash hands before Kiddush, because he needs to wash hands another time to perform the dipping, and the first berachah will be in vain, etc.; and Beit Yosef wondered on this: what interruption is there more on Pesach than Shabbat and Yom Tov? And it appears there is a dispute, for it is stated in the chapter of Arvei Pesachim: if he washed hands at the first dipping, he washes hands at the second dipping. And they explain the reason: since he needs to say the Haggadah and Hallel, he diverted his attention and touched an unclean place. And Tosafot explained: this second dipping is not precise, for it is after HaMotzi; rather it refers to washing for the meal — for non-sacred [meat] does not require intention, it teaches us; and one must emend somewhat in Mordechai in that which he wrote "because he needs," etc.; and it should read "therefore he needs," and the reading is: one should not wash before Kiddush on account of the meal on Pesach; and he brings proof as they say that one must wash again for bread because he interrupted between the first washing with the Haggadah and Hallel; and if so, if he washes hands before Kiddush, all the more so the Haggadah and Hallel will be considered an interruption before the eating of matzah; and even without the Hagah one can explain thus, because in any case he needs to wash hands for bread — thus there is interruption here; and that which he mentioned to perform the dipping follows the language of the Gemara, and in the Gemara it is not precise as written in the name of Tosafot. And Rashal wrote in his order that one should wash hands before, so as not to change from other Kiddushim of the year; but nevertheless he should bring himself to obligation of washing by pouring on his feet and rubbing, so that he should be obligated to wash from before Kiddush and not bless al netilat yadayim but rather Asher Yatzar; and if so, for dipping he does not need washing, for this dipping is not better than actual eating — for all year Kiddush is not an interruption and he eats through washing before Kiddush, all the more so dipping; and Maharach z"l required washing again for the first dipping, and I do not know the remedy in any matter for this extra washing before Kiddush on Pesach; for if on account of not changing from the rest of the year — behold he changes anyway, for now he does not bless al netilat yadayim and all year he blesses; and further, this remedy spoiled it, for when another sees this one washing he thinks he also blesses on it as the rest of the year, and in truth it is not fitting for him to bless now on Pesach because of the interruption as above; therefore the more correct [view] is as Rama wrote according to Mordechai, and it is the simple custom that they wash only until the first dipping. And that which Rashal wrote that one should not change from all year — I say: would that they would do so all year, to wash after Kiddush as written siman 471 seif 9:
turei-zahav/2:_: And he does not bless after it on the vine, etc., because he relies on what he will bless at the end of Grace after Meals — and see siman 474:
turei-zahav/4:א: (א) Or salt water. And if it falls on Shabbat he should prepare the salt water before Shabbat and not make it on Shabbat, as written siman 321 seif 1; and if he did not make it before Shabbat and he has no vinegar, salt water should be made in small quantity, as written siman 321:
turei-zahav/4:ב: (ב) And they are accustomed with meat and egg. For meat they are accustomed to take a foreleg on account of "outstretched arm," and it is a remembrance of the Pesach that was roasted on a spit; therefore they roast on coals. And an egg is a remembrance of the festival offering that they offered on the 14th and ate with the Pesach. And egg is the language of beya in Aramaic — meaning, the Merciful One seeks to redeem us. And Rashal wrote: the Ashkenaz custom to roast the meat and egg is because they do not eat them and keep them for the second night; and this custom is against the Talmud's custom — see chapter of Arvei Pesachim; and it is fitting to divide for each and they should be cooked, for it is impossible roasted; and I did not see in the Talmud from this that one must eat them; rather somewhat the opposite appears, for Rava said meat need not be raised; and not only that, but it appears as eating consecrated [meat] outside [the Temple]. Rashi explained: of the two cooked dishes — when he says "the Pesach that our forefathers ate," he should not raise the meat that is a remembrance of the Pesach; behold it is forbidden to make raising with this meat, lest it appear as if he consecrated it while alive; and even though he says that our forefathers ate, it implies we have no Pesach — nevertheless it is forbidden to raise; if so, when he eats them and divides them and says remembrance of the Pesach, there is certainly more reason to be concerned for this; and further Rashbam and Tosafot wrote in the name of R' Chananel that the meat should be roasted — thus they do not eat; also from what Rama wrote that the egg they are accustomed to cook, the reason appears for this intention: the meat that they leave for remembrance they do not eat then, for it is only on account of remembrance of the Pesach; but the egg has another reason on account of mourning for the Temple, as Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Kol Bo; and if so they eat the egg in the manner of mourners in Bava Metzia. And they are accustomed to cook many eggs on that night for this reason, as Rama wrote siman 477; and therefore the egg should specifically be cooked, because they do not eat roasted on Pesach nights, as Rashal wrote as above — the custom of our forefathers is correct that they do not eat the meat, and the egg they eat; for without remembrance of the festival offering it has a reason on account of mourning, as written; and in siman 477 it will be explained that there is no prohibition of roasted on egg or fish — see there:
turei-zahav/5:_: But not in their root. Mahariu wrote: meaning the small roots that branch to here and to there; but the large root in which the vegetable stands is included in the stalk; thus I saw many people who at the time of eating maror take their vegetable, and at the time of wrapping take the stalk — and this has no reason or logic; for one should take the vegetable also at the time of wrapping, for he can eat well a k'zayit from it, for it does not distress as much as the stalk which has more strength:
turei-zahav/6:א: (א) He washes hands for the need of the first dipping. For everything whose dipping is in liquid requires netilah. From here there is open rebuke to those who are not careful all year to wash before eating something whose dipping is in liquid — how is this night different from all the days of the year? And if he comes to purify himself more on this night, he should be careful at least on the ten days of repentance when everyone is careful to eat bread of a Jew specifically; but certainly here there is only lack of carefulness, and they do not scrutinize to equalize their measures:
turei-zahav/6:ב: (ב) And he should not bless on the washing. Tur wrote, and the Rambam wrote that nowadays one need not wash for something whose dipping is in liquid; therefore he would not bless al netilat yadayim on the first dipping — and likewise the author of Ittur, and I disagree; and likewise the Geonim that one must bless; and likewise Rosh in the name of Rashi; and one who wishes to fulfill doubt should bring himself to obligation of washing from another side, such as pouring water and rubbing. And the Rambam's reason: because washing is not on account of residue of terumah as with bread, but on account of cleanliness; and now we are not careful about cleanliness, as Tosafot wrote in the chapter of Arvei Pesachim; and Beit Yosef wrote that that which I disagree, his words are not correct, for since it is a dispute whether washing is required, it is better not to bless, end of his words. He further challenged that which Tur wrote "pour water and rub" — this thing does not bring him to berachah of al netilat yadayim per the Rosh in siman 7; and I disagree: Tur did not write "I disagree" on the berachah but on that which he wrote there is no obligation of washing nowadays; also in that which he wrote "one who wishes to fulfill doubt" — it refers to washing, not to the berachah; for if we say washing is not required for this, there is prohibition to wash, for it is arrogance, like one who washes hands for fruits — he is among the arrogant because washing is not needed there, the same here; therefore he wrote that he should bring himself to washing through rubbing, and by necessity he is obligated in berachah of al netilat yadayim, since something whose dipping is in liquid has similarity to bread; thus one who poured water and rubbed and comes to eat this thing — all agree there is obligation of washing as with bread without rubbing; and in this all agree, since there are two factors elevating obligation of washing; and it is as one who wishes to learn in siman 7 — a pity, nevertheless Beit Yosef and Shulchan Aruch ruled well not to bless on this and not to heed that this berachah is written in all siddurim; and likewise Tosafot in the chapter of Arvei Pesachim page 115: one who blesses blesses a berachah in vain; and in all siddurim it is written to bless on washing — and it does not appear, end of his words. And one should greatly wonder that he wrote on this night because of the obligation of the festival one should bless, and all year he himself wrote in siman 158 that one should not bless — and this thing is not correct at all to obligate berachah at one time more than another; therefore one should not bless at all as all year. And the reason for this dipping — Rashi and Rashbam [explain] on account of recognition, because people are not accustomed to eat vegetable before the meal, and the children will ask about it; and the apparent answer will be for them: if he had dipped only the second of maror, it would not have been recognizable that it was on account of a mitzvah, but in the manner of people to dip during the meal; therefore they enacted to dip before the meal, for thereby they hint that the dipping does not come on account of the meal, and it is a sign for the second dipping, which is also not on account of the meal but a rabbinic mitzvah, as above according to Rashi and Rambam:
turei-zahav/6:ג: (ג) Less than a k'zayit. Because if he eats a k'zayit he will be obligated to bless Borei nafashot, and there is a dispute whether he is obligated to bless it on the first dipping; therefore it is better he eat in a manner where there is no obligation at all. And the dispute is between R' Yitzchak and Rashbam: R' Yitzchak holds that the Haggadah and Hallel are an interruption between the dipping and the meal, as is written regarding washing that one must wash again for the meal, as written in seif 1 — the same for blessing acharonah on the dipping, and the Grace after Meals of the meal does not exempt it; but Rashbam holds as the Rosh explained: only for washing is the Haggadah considered an interruption, lest he touched an unclean place in between; but for blessing acharonah, no — just as one need not bless Borei peri ha'adamah on maror because he is exempted by the berachah he made at the first dipping, so too for blessing acharonah of the first dipping he is exempt, for it is related to the meal and as if he ate during the meal. And R' Yitzchak holds: not on account of this reason is he exempt from Borei peri ha'adamah and blessing acharonah on maror, but maror itself is related to the meal and exempted by HaMotzi and Grace after Meals; but the first dipping has no relation to the meal because of the interruption of Haggadah and Hallel. And it appears that in this dispute there is also a dispute regarding blessing acharonah of the first cups: for R' Yitzchak one must bless, and for Rashbam not:
turei-zahav/7:_: Why is this night different. Tur wrote that one should not say "we are not obligated to dip," etc., for it implies that on this night we are obligated to dip — and this is not so, for one is not obligated to dip except on account of recognition for children; rather he should say "we do not dip," etc. And in our Gemara it states "obligated to dip" — and it requires study, for it is an error: It is written in Maharil that the large piece should be taken for afikoman and not less than half — meaning the small portion; and a reason can be given for this, because that half of afikoman is the essence of the mitzvah that he eats at the end: Mordechai wrote that one must say "and we shall eat there of the sacrifices and of the Pesach offerings," for they eat first of the festival offering, which is the sacrifice; but the Pesach is eaten on the full [stomach]. And Mahariu wrote that if Pesach falls on Shabbat one must say that night "of the Pesach offerings and of the sacrifices," for the festival offering is not offered on Shabbat. Tur wrote that one should say "and we shall thank You, a new song," and not say "a new shirah," since he speaks of the future redemption which is masculine language, as stated in the midrash, end of his words. And in the text in our siddurim it is written "and we shall say before Him a new shirah, Halleluyah" — this too is not correct, since he says "v'ne'emar," it refers by necessity to the future redemption. And in some books they did not write at all this "new shirah," and that is correct; for in truth it refers to the redemption that passed, for they recite the Egyptian Hallel. And in Mordechai of the elders of Mahari bar Betzalel z"l it was vocalized "v'ne'emar" with segol, and this is more correct; and it is fitting to say "a new shirah," for when "ne'emar" is with segol it is past tense:
